continuity.arc_goal: Design the next evolution of Restate's process model — from isolated virtual objects to a connected graph of durable processes with structural relationships, efficient communication primitives, and real-time observability. Sessions 1-3 built SSE infrastructure and planned repartitioning. Session 4 pivoted to explore a larger vision: process composition primitives unified with an edge model, ownership via spawn, and a clean taxonomy of graph communication node types.

progress_update.summary: We squashed 42 commits into one, validated (fmt/clippy/tests pass), pushed to `live-state-poc` branch. Then conducted a deep design session exploring Restate as durable language-agnostic Erlang/OTP. Produced an RFC proposing process composition primitives — unified edge model, ownership via spawn, reactive edges, broadcast channels, and output streams. Iterated through multiple rounds of critique, arriving at a clean taxonomy of four graph node types: LiveState, Broadcast, LiveAggregation, and Stream.
progress_update.goal: Design the next evolution of Restate's process model — from isolated virtual objects to a connected graph of durable processes with structural relationships, efficient communication primitives, and real-time observability.
accomplished: Squashed 42 commits into 1, validated (cargo fmt/clippy/nextest all pass), pushed to `live-state-poc` branch on origin
Produced comprehensive design summary of the live-state-poc SSE architecture
Wrote RFC: Process Composition Primitives (unified edge model collapsing OTP links/monitors/groups into one primitive)
Iterated RFC through critique — identified edges vs channels as structurally distinct primitives
Arrived at 4 graph node types: LiveState (coalescable, one→many), Broadcast (ordered, one→many), LiveAggregation (coalescable, many→one), Stream (ordered, many→one)
progress_update.now: Refining the taxonomy of graph communication primitives — LiveState vs Broadcast vs LiveAggregation vs Stream. Just established naming conventions where 'Live' prefix = coalescable/latest-value semantics.
next_steps: Update RFC with the four node types taxonomy and edges-vs-channels distinction
Design the broadcast channel as partition-aware infrastructure backed by Bifrost
Prototype ctx.emit() + invocation introspection as the highest-value, lowest-complexity next step
Consider state migration (onUpgrade) as independent high-value feature
constraints: Cross-partition edges are the hardest unsolved implementation problem
Broadcast channels need partition-local subscriber lists (not edge traversal at send time)
Reactive aggregation with algebraic guarantees may be over-designed for near-term needs
Sessions 1-3 built SSE infrastructure for state streaming; this is a foundation but Session 4 pivoted to larger vision rather than completing SSE repartitioning
decisions: Edges model structure (relationships, ownership, graph traversal). Channels model communication (message delivery, fan-out). Two distinct primitives, not one.
A 'Link' is two directed edges created atomically — no special Link type needed
A 'Group' is just a high in-degree node — no special Group type needed
Four graph node types: LiveState, Broadcast, LiveAggregation, Stream — distinguished by compaction policy and data flow direction
Ownership (ctx.spawn) vs subscription (ctx.edge) distinguished by edge property, not type
ctx.emit() and invocation introspection are highest-value, lowest-complexity features to ship next
open_questions: Should LiveAggregation fold functions be limited to built-ins or support user-defined?
How do broadcast channel partition-local subscriber lists interact with repartitioning?
What's the minimum SDK surface to validate the edge model?
Should the RFC be updated with the full four-node taxonomy before broader review?
risks: Vision is compelling but far from implementation — risk of designing the second floor while foundation is unproven
Cross-partition edge consistency may require distributed transactions or weaker guarantees than expected
OTP analogies may import assumptions that don't apply to durable execution (ephemeral vs persistent processes)
